chunks: Abu Ali Al-Ash'ari, from Muhammad ibn Abd al-Jabbar, from Muhammad ibn Ismail, from Ali ibn al-Nu'man, from Suwayd al-Qalla', from Ayoub ibn al-Hurr, from Abu Bakr al-Hadrami, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

I said to him, 'Indeed, Alqamah ibn Muhammad bequeathed to me that I should emancipate a neck on his behalf, so I emancipated a woman on his behalf. Is that sufficient for him, or should I emancipate on his behalf from my own wealth?' He said, 'It is sufficient.'
Then he said to me, 'Indeed, Fatima, the mother of my son, bequeathed that I should emancipate a neck on her behalf, so I emancipated a woman on her behalf.'

key_terms.أُمَّ ابْنِي: Mother of my son (referring to Fatima al-Ma'sumah)
key_terms.رَقَبَةً: A neck (referring to a slave, male or female, to be emancipated)

ai.seo_question: Is freeing a female slave sufficient to fulfill a bequest for freeing a 'neck'?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi establishes the juristic principle that the specific term 'raqabah' (neck/slave) in bequests is fulfilled by emancipating any slave, regardless of gender, as confirmed by Imam al-Sadiq (AS). It highlights the practical application of fiday (redemption) in Shia fiqh, where the act of liberation satisfies the deceased's debt without requiring the exact demographic specified if the general category is met. This ruling underscores the flexibility in fulfilling religious obligations through charitable acts, reinforcing the spiritual value of manumission as a means of expiation and charity.
